title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
gist: After visiting Data Center Alley in Ashburn, Virginia, the author argues the data center backlash is largely about electricity and its physical consequences, not a proxy culture war as Big Tech frames it. Gas-fired behind-the-meter power and multi-gigawatt scale push builds toward sparse areas, abroad, or even space.

themes.theme: Backlash is about power, not culture war

insights.claim: OpenAI's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane wrote two days after the midterms that data centers have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power and people losing control over their futures.
insights.speaker: Chris Lehane
insights.so_what: Shows how the industry frames opposition.
insights.quote: have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures

insights.claim: The author concludes after days in Data Center Alley that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits; the industry can improve its image but cannot escape the physical consequences of its electricity appetite.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: PR and community-benefit fixes will not fully defuse opposition.

insights.claim: Activist Elena Schlossberg says the fight was always about power and that the industry's culture war framing frustrates her.
insights.speaker: Elena Schlossberg
insights.so_what: Local activists reject the proxy narrative.

insights.claim: Big Tech's culture war framing obscures that there is only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Opposition is rational and persistent, not mere misinformation.

insights.claim: Fears of job losses, existential risk and concentrated corporate power and misinformation also fuel the backlash, though most facilities use far less water than many people think.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Backlash has multiple drivers, but the water complaint is overstated.

insights.claim: The average data center operating in this part of Virginia has a power capacity of 54 megawatts, more than the power draw of Denver International Airport.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Even the mature-market average is large relative to local infrastructure.

insights.claim: Virginia protests have produced state rules requiring data centers to fully pay for new transmission lines rather than spreading costs across other ratepayers.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Cost allocation rules raise data center capex and set a precedent for other states.

insights.claim: Developers are preparing for rules that would cut data centers off from grid power during peak demand.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Curtailment requirements push demand toward onsite generation and flexibility.

insights.claim: Schlossberg worries a strained grid will lead to more diesel generator use or to Dominion Energy expanding fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables.
insights.speaker: Elena Schlossberg
insights.so_what: Utilities leaning on gas benefits gas suppliers and complicates emissions goals.

insights.claim: Most AI data centers being built outside Loudoun County are not grid connected; they are going to rural areas with little grid infrastructure and bringing their own natural-gas turbine power, with diesel backup.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Gas turbine demand and onsite generation are core enablers of the AI buildout.

insights.claim: Anthropic has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines, described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: AI labs are becoming direct buyers of power generation equipment.

insights.claim: The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts, while ideal facilities are about 6,000 megawatts, the estimated draw of Chicago.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Required scale exceeds what most grids can serve, driving self-generation.

insights.claim: Self-generating power at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and gas turbines emit air pollutants, with diesel generators worse.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Local air-quality and permitting conflicts are a growing risk for developers.

insights.claim: Elon Musk violated air quality laws when setting up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the EPA, an example of companies becoming horrible neighbors in the rush to build.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Regulatory enforcement risk for fast-moving builds.

insights.claim: A developer says industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Power, not politics, is the binding constraint on AI capacity.

insights.claim: If data centers need onsite power, they will go where the fewest people can resist them, such as the Permian Basin where gas pipelines are accessible and populations are sparse.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Gas-rich sparse regions could capture AI infrastructure investment.

insights.claim: Google announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia, showing companies may try their chances abroad.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Capex is shifting to jurisdictions with fewer constraints.

insights.claim: Elon Musk posted hours after the midterm results that data centers in space look pretty appealing right now.
insights.speaker: Elon Musk
insights.so_what: Signals how far industry is willing to go to escape terrestrial limits.
insights.quote: Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now

insights.claim: Newly elected politicians' actual stances on data centers may be less negative than the ones they campaigned on.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Rhetoric may overstate eventual policy restrictions.
